blocks.text: When her people confront Maryam ﵍ with her infant, the Qur'an gives their address, the sister of Aaron, joined to a defense of her parents' honor (Qur'an 19:27-28). Aaron the prophet, brother of Moses ﵇, lived about a thousand years before her. Christian critics say the Qur'an has confused two women, Maryam ﵍ the mother of Isa ﵇ and Miriam the sister of Moses ﵇, and rolled them into one. If she was not Aaron's ﵇ sister, the charge concludes, the verse should never have said sister.
blocks.observation: Rendered opening states the charge: the address is "joined to a defense of her parents' honor" while critics read a confusion of two women; it sets the debate's object.

blocks.text: The surah's own story answers the family questions in order. Her father was Imran, and he is not the Amram who fathered Moses ﵇ and Aaron ﵇ a thousand years earlier; the two men share one ancient name, carried by the custom of naming children after the righteous. Sister of Aaron rides the same custom and the language's kinship grammar. The school's recorded readings, the Prophet's ﷺ own answer at Najran, the lexicons, the poetry they preserve, and the Gospel's kinship words all carry it.
blocks.observation: Revised in the council batch; the frame paragraph now reads "The surah's own story answers the family questions in order" without the deleted vow-and-lot preview, and renders as two sentences.

blocks.text: The Imams ﵈, the twelve of the Ahl al-Bayt whom the school follows, read the verse this way from the beginning. Ali ibn Ibrahim al-Qummi (d.329 AH) narrates the scene and explains the address inside it. Al-Sharif al-Murtada (d.436) gave a session of his Amali to the readings of the verse. The objection reached the Prophet ﷺ in his own lifetime from the Christians of Najran, and his answer has chains in the Sunni and the Shia books alike.
blocks.observation: Revised witness paragraph rendering the calendar fix, "Ali ibn Ibrahim al-Qummi (d.329 AH) narrates the scene", alongside al-Murtada's session and the Najran provenance.

blocks.text: Maryam's ﵍ father was Imran and her mother Hanna. In al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq ﵇ reports Allah's promise to Imran of a messenger son, and that Imran told his wife Hanna, she being the mother of Maryam. Al-Hilli (d.726) names the couple the same way (Idah al-Mukhalafa, p.204). The Qur'an opens her birth story with this woman's vow (Qur'an 3:35) and calls Maryam the daughter of Imran (Qur'an 66:12), naming the man of her own century.
blocks.observation: Rendered premise card one grounds the parents in "In al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq reports Allah's promise to Imran of a messenger son" with the Qur'an verse pair.

blocks.text: She was vowed to the sanctuary, and Zakariyya ﵇, the husband of her sister, won her charge by lot. Her mother vowed the child as a muharrar, dedicated to the mosque for life. The custodians cast lots over her care, and the lot fell to Zakariyya, whom the school's report identifies as the husband of her sister (Nur al-Thaqalayn, vol.1, p.336). The Qur'an itself records the casting of the pens (Qur'an 3:44) and Zakariyya's charge (Qur'an 3:37). Guardianship by vow and lot leaves paternity where the Qur'an puts it, with Imran.
blocks.observation: Rendered premise card two: "Her mother vowed the child as a muharrar", the custodians cast lots, and the lot fell to Zakariyya, the husband of her sister.

blocks.text: Her Imran is not the Amram of the Torah. The Torah's Amram fathered Aaron ﵇ and Moses ﵇ in the Exodus generation, a millennium and more before Maryam. Her father is the Imran of Zakariyya's century. The names are one name recurring, by the custom the Prophet ﷺ gave at Najran, that the Children of Israel named their children after their prophets and the righteous. The Bible never names Mary's father.
blocks.observation: Rendered premise card three separates the men: the Torah's Amram belongs to "the Exodus generation, a millennium and more before Maryam".

blocks.text: Sister of Aaron is a kinship address, and no reading in the surveyed record takes it for a womb sisterhood. The school's exegetes recorded the readings. A righteous namesake of her own people, with the Najran answer behind it. A woman of Aaron's ﵇ line, stated by al-Murtada among the readings and glossed by Muqatil at the verse. A wicked namesake the crowd reached for as an insult, in al-Qummi's narration. A righteous brother who shared neither of her parents. On none of them does the verse name a womb-sister of Moses' ﵇ brother, and that is the only reading the confusion charge needs.
blocks.observation: Rendered premise four carries the corrected attribution: the lineage reading "stated by al-Murtada among the readings and glossed by Muqatil at the verse", with the enumeration and surveyed-record scope unchanged.

blocks.text: No recorded reading makes the verse name a womb-sister of Aaron the prophet. From Premise 1 and Premise 2, the family is fixed. Her father Imran, her mother Hanna, her guardian the husband of her sister, chosen by the sanctuary's lot. From Premise 3, the father is a man of her own century whose ancient name the custom explains. From Premise 4, the address carries kinship in the language's own grammar, the Imams' ﵈ usage, the lexicons, the poetry they preserve, and the Gospel's kinship words. The charge needs sister to mean one womb, and no part of the evidence gives it that rule.
blocks.observation: Rendered conclusion card, "No recorded reading makes the verse name a womb-sister of Aaron the prophet", deriving the thesis from the four premises above it.

blocks.text: The report attests that the verse was heard and tested within the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime by Christians who knew the scriptures the charge draws on. It also preserves the answer in the Prophet's own words. The Children of Israel used to attach their children to their prophets and righteous men, and an address by a saint's name follows that custom. The same report stands in Sahih Muslim's Kitab al-Adab, among the most strictly graded Sunni collections. The records of the exchange in both communities' books carry it from al-Mughira.

blocks.text: The report grants the charge its identification. The Aaron of the address is Aaron the prophet ﵇, brother of Moses ﵇, and that much is what the Prophet's ﷺ report gives. The lineage gloss is Muqatil's own, that brother-of in the Qur'an's mouth means one of their descendants and their kind, exactly the Hud and Salih construction he cites.

blocks.text: Muqatil's standing is the obvious objection. He is an early transmitter whom the later critics graded harshly, and a hostile reader will say so; the school's case does not lean on him. Al-Murtada, the hardest critic of reports his generation produced, cites him as one reading among several. Every other reading carries the same conclusion from other evidence, through the Qur'an's own usage, the naming custom from Najran, the lexicons, and the living speech. If Muqatil fails as a witness, the idiom still rests on that evidence; if he holds, he carries the report that names the Aaron of the address.
blocks.observation: Rendered qualification closes "he carries the report that names the Aaron of the address", keeping the both-ways conditional without crediting Muqatil with the Prophet's sentence for the idiom.

Behind the number stands a people who named their sons after the saints of the line so consistently that a righteous Harun could die with a crowd of his namesakes behind his bier. A woman of that people, addressed by the same name, is being measured against the house's standard of piety.

blocks.text: On this reading the crowd named no genealogy of hers. They cut her with a comparison to a notorious man of their own generation, a Harun known for sin. The address is an insult, and an insult needs a reference the audience shares. A Harun of their own day gives them one, and the verse reports their words without endorsing their sneer. On this reading too, the thousand years the confusion charge needs are gone, since a contemporary Harun stands inside Maryam's ﵍ own world. Al-Qummi's Harun is a wicked man and the exegetes' Harun is a saint, and the disagreement between the reports is real. The two readings still share one presupposition, that the name Harun sat on many men of her people, and that breadth of the name is what the naming custom rests on. A name forty thousand men carried sat on sinners and saints alike, and a crowd reaching for the house's name could reach for a notorious namesake or a holy one. The two readings answer different questions, al-Qummi's namesake telling which man the crowd reached for, and the lineage readings telling whose house the name carries.

blocks.text: Al-Balaghi presses the inference at its strongest, that the shared lineage runs whole and Maryam ﵍ is paternally Aaronic. The Gospel itself says less, and that much is certain. It makes Maryam ﵍ a blood relative of a woman of Aaron's house. Which line the shared blood runs through, father's or mother's, the tradition itself divides, and John of Damascus (d.749) draws the maternal Aaronic line in his Homily on the Nativity, Joachim of Judah and David for her father's side, an Aaronic, Levitical house for her mother's. The tradition that presses the charge carries, in its own memory, the Aaronic kin the address names.

blocks.text: The counter-branch itself concedes the custom. Ibn al-Athir grants that she was of the line of Aaron, so it has been said. He then explains the address by the naming custom, they were called after the righteous, which is the Prophet's ﷺ own answer from Najran. One branch of the tradition holds her of Aaron's ﵇ blood, with sisterhood naming the line. The other holds her of Judah, with the address following the naming custom. A third branch, on which the crowd's words claim a womb shared with the brother of Moses ﵇, appears nowhere in the surveyed readings.

blocks.text: Abraham says to Lot, we be brethren, and Lot is his nephew, so the brother-word covers a named man who shares no womb with Abraham. These verses carry the form the surveyed Arabic record does not attest separately, a kinship word joined to one named individual. The Hebrew ach carries kinsman as easily as brother, and the Gospel's Greek inherits the breadth. The assembly that confronted Maryam ﵍ spoke that Hebrew or its Aramaic daughter, and the Qur'an recites their address in Arabic. The objection that seventh-century Arabic cannot tell what first-century Israelites meant is answered from the charge's own scriptures, which carry the same wide kinship field in the crowd's own language.

blocks.text: The Torah's history uses the same words for nations a thousand years apart. Moses ﵇ writes to Edom centuries after Esau and names Israel the brother nation, the two brothers Jacob and Esau standing at the head of both lines. A descendant people is a brother people, generation after generation, in the very scriptures the charge appeals to.

blocks.text: A hostile reader may hand this verse to the charge instead, since Miriam truly was Aaron's ﵇ sister by the womb. Miriam is Moses' ﵇ sister too, and the Torah titles her by the house's priest, the sister of Aaron ﵇, the ascription that carries the house's honor. A woman who could have been named by the more famous brother is named by the one whose line carried the priesthood, and the crowd's address makes the same choice a thousand years later. The title the Torah gives the first woman of that name is the address the crowd gave Maryam ﵍.

blocks.text: Hud shares no womb with the whole nation Ad, and Salih shares none with every man of Thamud. The Qur'an sends Shu'ayb to Madyan in the same register (Qur'an 7:85). It calls each prophet the brother of the nation he was sent to because he is of their stock and their kind.

blocks.text: Daughter of Imran shows the kinship word joined to a named individual, for descent. Brother of Ad and brother of Thamud show the kinship word joined to a collective, for belonging. What 19:28 writes, a feminine kinship word joined to the house's named saint, composes those two registers. No independent Arabic example of this exact form, a kinship word joined to one named man, survives in the surveyed record. The two registers are each attested, and the verse's own early exegetes read the composition without strain, Muqatil glossing it at the verse itself and al-Murtada stating it with the Tamim parallel. The Qur'an spends the same words more loosely still. It calls the believers brothers wherever they live (Qur'an 49:10), and the reckless spendthrifts brothers of the devils (Qur'an 17:27), where no blood is in question.
blocks.observation: Rendered register-composition paragraph with its limit: no independent example of the exact form "survives in the surveyed record".

blocks.text: Christian tradition traces the Lord's family to David, and Matthew opens his Gospel with the claim. Jerome answered that they were kin, the sons of Mary the wife of Alphaeus, called Mary of Clopas. He takes her for the sister or kinswoman of the Lord's mother, so that sons of the mother's sister can be called the Lord's brethren (Jerome, Against Helvidius, 383, chs. 14-16). The older tradition holds the Virgin ever virgin, a title the Second Council of Constantinople confessed in 553. John of Damascus (d.749) gives Mary a double lineage in his Homily on the Nativity, Davidic on her father's side, Aaronic on her mother's. The canon's own family register thus runs through the same wide kinship words, and the strongest Christian readings of them are readings of kinship. The kinship words carry the range the charge denies to Arabic.
